newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Montenegrans would oppose Serb dominance.
newsitem.headline: Montenegrans would oppose Serb dominance.

text.p: The reformist faction of the Montenegrin Democratic Party of Socialists (DPS) vowed on Friday to block any constitutional changes that might lead to the political dominance of Serbia, the bigger partner in the new Balkan federation.

"We shall not give up. Everyone has a right to a choice, but we shall be against any changes of the constitution," Montenegrin parliament speaker Svetozar Marovic told reporters after Slobodan Milosevic was elected Yugoslavia's president. A row between Serbia's ruling Socialist Party (SPS) and a reformist faction of DPS first arose when SPS called for constitutional amendments so that Milosevic could be elected by a popular vote instead by the parliament.

Analysts said such a move would help Milosevic sidestep control which the federal parliament holds over the president and dampen hopes that a Montenegrin would take the presidential office once it is Montenegro's turn to nominate a candidate.
Montenegrin reformist Prime Minister Milo Djukanovic was confident the parliament could not vote constitutional changes without Montenegro supporting them.

"I do not think it is possible. I believe Montenegrin deputies in the Upper House of the Yugoslav parliament who protect our interests will act responsibly. Not a single political force in Montenegro wants amendments," he said.
Some analysts feared Milosevic could engineer the amendments without consulting the federal parliament.
Montenegrin politicians insisted this was impossible because the president's moves were under parliament's control.
Earlier this year Montenegrin reformists, eager to get out of international isolation, called for more democracy, privatisation and quick return to international financial institutions.

They have also threatened to seek a deal with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) independently, as Yugoslavia remained outside the IMF and other institutions until it met several political conditions.
These included cooperation with The Hague war crimes tribunal, respect for human rights in its mostly Albanian Kosovo province and speeding up talks on dividing former Yugoslav assets.

Montenegro, the junior partner to Serbia in a Balkan federation that remained after the violent break-up of Yugoslavia in 1991, is home to some 650,000 people and heavily reliant on tourism, iron and aluminium industries.
It generates five percent of Yugoslavia's GDP, but refused to wait for Serbia to begin with radical economic reforms and launched its own voucher privatisation model.
